nodes.name: Microstate
nodes.statement: A microstate is one exact arrangement of the positions and momenta of every particle in a system.

nodes.name: Macrostate
nodes.statement: A macrostate is described by a few bulk quantities such as energy, volume and particle number. Many different microstates share the same macrostate.

nodes.name: Multiplicity Ω
nodes.statement: The multiplicity Ω of a macrostate is the number of microstates consistent with it.

nodes.name: Equal a priori probabilities
nodes.statement: In an isolated system at equilibrium, every accessible microstate is equally likely.

nodes.name: Gibbs entropy
nodes.statement: Gibbs entropy is S = −k Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ, summed over microstates with probabilities pᵢ.

nodes.name: Boltzmann entropy
nodes.statement: Entropy is S = k ln Ω, where k is Boltzmann's constant, about 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

nodes.name: Entropy is additive
nodes.statement: For two independent systems the multiplicities multiply, Ω = Ω₁Ω₂. The logarithm turns this product into a sum, so S = S₁ + S₂.

nodes.name: Multiplicity grows exponentially
nodes.statement: Multiplicity grows roughly exponentially with particle number. For about 10²³ particles, the largest macrostates outnumber all others by astronomical factors.

nodes.name: Most probable macrostate
nodes.statement: Because all microstates are equally likely, a system is overwhelmingly likely to be found in the macrostate with the largest multiplicity.

nodes.name: Second law
nodes.statement: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases over time. It stays constant only in an ideal reversible process.

nodes.name: Statistical second law
nodes.statement: The second law is statistical. A drop in entropy by ΔS has a probability of roughly e^(−ΔS/k), which is negligible for any macroscopic change.

nodes.name: Equilibrium maximizes entropy
nodes.statement: An isolated system settles into the macrostate of maximum entropy and then stays there. That state is thermal equilibrium.

nodes.name: Clausius definition
nodes.statement: When heat δQ enters a system reversibly at temperature T, its entropy changes by dS = δQ/T.

nodes.name: Temperature from entropy
nodes.statement: Temperature is defined by 1/T = ∂S/∂E at fixed volume and particle number.

nodes.name: Heat flows hot to cold
nodes.statement: Heat flows by itself from a hotter body to a colder one. Moving energy E from hot to cold changes the total entropy by E(1/T_cold − 1/T_hot), which is positive.

nodes.name: Free expansion
nodes.statement: When a gas of N molecules expands into a vacuum to double its volume, Ω grows by a factor of 2ᴺ. Its entropy therefore rises by Nk ln 2 with no heat added.

nodes.name: Entropy of mixing
nodes.statement: Two different gases mix by themselves when the wall between them is removed, because the mixed state has vastly more microstates than the separated one.

nodes.name: Engines must reject heat
nodes.statement: A heat engine must dump some heat into a cold reservoir. Turning all the heat from a single reservoir into work would lower the total entropy.

nodes.name: Carnot limit
nodes.statement: No heat engine running between temperatures T_hot and T_cold can have an efficiency above 1 − T_cold/T_hot.

nodes.name: Local entropy can fall
nodes.statement: Entropy can decrease inside an open system, such as a freezer or a living cell, as long as more entropy is exported to the surroundings.

nodes.name: Life runs on low entropy
nodes.statement: Earth absorbs sunlight as relatively few high-energy photons and radiates about 20 times as many low-energy infrared photons. This export of entropy pays for the order of living things.

nodes.name: Low-entropy past
nodes.statement: The universe began in a state of very low entropy, so entropy has had room to rise ever since.

nodes.name: Arrow of time
nodes.statement: The microscopic laws of motion work the same forwards and backwards in time. The direction of everyday processes comes from entropy rising away from a low-entropy past.

nodes.name: Shannon entropy
nodes.statement: Shannon entropy H = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ measures missing information in bits. It has the same form as Gibbs entropy, differing only by the factor k ln 2.

nodes.name: Landauer's principle
nodes.statement: Erasing one bit of information releases at least kT ln 2 of heat into surroundings at temperature T.

nodes.name: Maxwell's demon fails
nodes.statement: A demon that sorts fast and slow molecules cannot beat the second law. Erasing its memory of the molecules produces at least as much entropy as the sorting removed.

nodes.name: Third law
nodes.statement: As temperature approaches absolute zero, the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero, because only a single microstate remains.
